claims.text: Unreinforced CoCrFeNi exhibits increasing friction and wear, especially at elevated temperatures.
The elevated-temperature wear of unreinforced CoCrFeNi results from limited intrinsic self-lubrication and wear resistance.
Adding ceramic and graphite particles to CoCrFeNi will produce a dual-phase or multiphase composite microstructure.
The proposed ceramic/graphite reinforcement will dynamically generate a stable self-lubricating tribofilm.
The ceramic/graphite-reinforced CoCrFeNi composite will lower both friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
A mixture containing approximately 10–20 wt% WC-type ceramic and graphite particles should be introduced into the CoCrFeNi matrix.
Hard ceramic particles provide dispersion strengthening and wear resistance.
Graphite particles contribute to formation of a lubricious carbon-based tribofilm during sliding.
At lower temperatures, ceramic reinforcement increases hardness and load-bearing capacity and thereby mitigates abrasive wear.
As temperature increases, graphite becomes tribologically active and generates a continuous lubricious tribofilm.
The graphite-derived tribofilm reduces interfacial shear strength, lowering friction and wear rate.
Synergy between the ceramic and graphite particles will maintain stable tribological performance across the full temperature range.
The reinforced composite will reduce coefficient of friction by approximately 20–30% relative to unreinforced CoCrFeNi.
The reinforced composite may reduce wear rate by approximately one order of magnitude relative to unreinforced CoCrFeNi.
The improvements will persist across varying loads and temperatures up to 800 °C.
The improvement will hold under moderate-to-high sliding loads in ambient or mildly oxidative environments.
Extreme oxidative environments or temperatures above 800 °C may undermine the proposed improvement.
Environmental changes can substantially alter the effectiveness of a self-lubricating tribological system.
The optimal reinforcement fraction and distribution, graphite activation temperature, and effect of particle agglomeration remain uncertain.
A controlled ball-on-disk comparison of reinforced and unreinforced CoCrFeNi can test the predicted reductions and the presence of a lubricious tribofilm.

contradictions.description: The intervention calls 10–20 wt% a 'volume fraction'; wt% is a mass fraction, so the loading specification is internally inconsistent.

The hypothesis specifies a dual-phase microstructure, whereas the structural mediator includes a CoCrFeNi matrix, ceramic particles, and graphite particles and therefore describes at least three distinct constituents unless 'dual-phase' is given a narrower definition.
